nodes.name: Gallager's redundancy bound for Huffman codes
nodes.statement:
Gallager \cite{Gallager78} introduced the
sibling property and proved $R<p_1+0.086$, reproved more simply by Ye and Yeung
\cite{YeYeung02}; Johnsen \cite{Johnsen80} improved the estimate for
$p_1\ge0.4$; and Capocelli, Giancarlo, and Taneja
\cite{CapocelliGiancarloTaneja86}, Capocelli and De~Santis
\cite{CapocelliDeSantis89,CapocelliDeSantis91}, Montgomery and Abrahams
\cite{MontgomeryAbrahams87}, and Manstetten \cite{Manstetten92} determined the
exact worst-case Huffman redundancy as a function of $p_1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Gallager 1978; Ye & Yeung 2002; Johnsen 1980; Capocelli et al.; Montgomery & Abrahams; Manstetten 1992
nodes.statement_short: Huffman redundancy is below $p_1+0.086$ (Gallager, via the sibling property); later sharpened to exact worst-case values as functions of $p_1$.

nodes.name: Source
nodes.statement:
A \emph{source} is a probability vector $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ with
$p_1\ge\cdots\ge p_n>0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$.
nodes.section: 2 Shannon--Fano Coding and the Fano Recursion

nodes.name: Binary Shannon--Fano (Fano) coding
nodes.statement:
The binary \emph{Shannon--Fano} code
\cite{Shannon48,Fano49} is the leaf code of the tree built by the following
recursion on contiguous blocks of the sorted list. A block consisting of a single
symbol is a leaf. A block $\{i,\dots,j\}$ of mass $M=\sum_{t=i}^{j}p_t$ is split
after a position $k$ ($i\le k<j$) into a left part $\{i,\dots,k\}$ (code bit $0$)
and a right part $\{k+1,\dots,j\}$ (code bit $1$), where $k$ minimises the
\emph{imbalance} $|m_L-m_R|$, $m_L=\sum_{t=i}^{k}p_t$, $m_R=M-m_L$; then recurse
on the two parts. We fix the convention that ties among minimising cuts are
broken toward the smaller left part; the code, and hence $R$, is then well
defined.
nodes.section: 2 Shannon--Fano Coding and the Fano Recursion
input: contiguous blocks of the sorted list
output: the leaf code of the tree
nodes.statement_short: Top-down coding: split each sorted block at the cut minimising the imbalance $|m_L-m_R|$ (ties to the smaller left part) and recurse.

nodes.name: Codeword length, expected length, entropy and redundancy
nodes.statement:
Let $\ell_i$ denote the depth of symbol $i$ in this tree (its codeword length),
$\mathbb E[l]=\sum_i p_i\ell_i$ the expected length, $\mathrm H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i$ the entropy, and $R = R(p) := \mathbb E[l]-\mathrm H(p)$
the \emph{redundancy}.
nodes.section: 2 Shannon--Fano Coding and the Fano Recursion
nodes.statement_short: Redundancy $R$ = expected codeword length minus entropy of the source.

nodes.name: Redundancy as a KL divergence
nodes.statement:
Since every internal node of the tree has two children,
the Kraft sum is exactly $1$, so $R=\sum_i p_i\bigl(\ell_i+\log_2 p_i\bigr)
=\mathrm D\bigl(p\,\|\,2^{-\ell}\bigr)\ge0$, where $\mathrm D$ denotes
Kullback--Leibler divergence.
nodes.section: 2 Shannon--Fano Coding and the Fano Recursion
assumptions: every internal node of the tree has two children
nodes.statement_short: Full binary tree gives Kraft sum 1, so $R=D(p\|2^{-\ell})\ge0$.

nodes.name: Entropy notation I, H_2, H
nodes.statement:
Throughout, $\mathrm I(p):=-p\log_2 p$ \textup{(}$\mathrm I(0)=0$\textup{)},
$\mathrm H_2(p):=\mathrm I(p)+\mathrm I(1-p)$ is the binary entropy function
\textup{(}concave, $\mathrm H_2(0)=\mathrm H_2(1)=0$, $\mathrm H_2(\tfrac12)=1$\textup{)}, and for a
nonnegative vector we write
$\mathrm H(p_1,\dots,p_k):=\sum_i \mathrm I(p_i)$.
nodes.section: 2 Shannon--Fano Coding and the Fano Recursion
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $\mathrm I(p)=-p\log_2 p$, binary entropy $\mathrm H_2$, and $\mathrm H$ of a nonnegative vector.

nodes.name: Balance function kappa and c_3
nodes.statement:
The envelope is built from the balance function
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \kappa(d)&\ :=\ 1-\mathrm H_2\!\Bigl(\tfrac{1+d}{2}\Bigr)\quad(d\in[-1,1]),\\
  c_3&\ :=\ \kappa(\tfrac13)\ =\ \tfrac53-\log_23 .
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.statement_short: Balance function $\kappa(d)=1-\mathrm H_2((1+d)/2)$ and constant $c_3=\kappa(1/3)$.

nodes.name: Basic properties of kappa
nodes.statement: The function $\kappa$ is even and convex, with $\kappa(0)=0$ and $\kappa(\pm1)=1$.

nodes.name: Constants lambda and C
nodes.statement_short: Define $\lambda=1+5\kappa(1/5)$ and $C=c_3+(\lambda-1)/3$.

nodes.name: Definition of lambda and C
nodes.label: eq:constants

nodes.name: Closed form of C
nodes.statement: C=4-\tfrac53\log_25 .
nodes.statement_short: The $\log_2 3$ terms cancel: $C=4-\frac53\log_2 5$.
nodes.label: eq:cancel

nodes.name: Envelope curves K, V, W_iso, F_ell, Pi, Theta, N
nodes.statement:
Put
\[
  K:=\frac{1+C}{2}=\frac52-\frac56\log_25,\qquad
  V(x):=2-x-\mathrm H_2(x),
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
  W_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)&:=1-\mathrm H_2(x)+(1-x)K,\\
  F_\ell(x)&:=\frac{5-x}{3}+\frac{2-x}{3}C
  -\mathrm H\Bigl(x,\frac{1-2x}{3},\frac{2-x}{3}\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Pi(x)&:=\frac32+\frac{C}{2}-x-\mathrm I(x)-\mathrm I\left(\frac12-x\right),\\
  \Theta(x)&:=\frac{4+2x}{3}+\frac{2(1-x)}{3}K
   -\mathrm H\Bigl(x,\frac{1-x}{3},\frac{2(1-x)}{3}\Bigr),\\
  N(x)&:=3-3x-\mathrm H(x,x,x,1-3x).
\end{aligned}
\]
also_stated_at:
The three curves of the quarter-window ceiling
are
\begin{align*}
  \Pi(p_1)&:=\tfrac32+\tfrac{C}2-p_1-\mathrm I(p_1)-\mathrm I\bigl(\tfrac12-p_1\bigr),\\
  \Theta(p_1)&:=\tfrac{4+2p_1}{3}+\tfrac{2(1-p_1)}{3}\,K
   -\mathrm H\Bigl(p_1,\tfrac{1-p_1}{3},\tfrac{2(1-p_1)}{3}\Bigr),\\
  N(p_1)&:=3-3p_1-3\mathrm I(p_1)-\mathrm I(1-3p_1)\\
   &\ =\ 3-3p_1-\mathrm H\bigl(p_1,p_1,p_1,1-3p_1\bigr).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the cap $K=(1+C)/2$ and the six curves $V,W_{iso},F_\ell,\Pi,\Theta,N$ that make up the envelope.

nodes.name: Auxiliary zeros r_1, q_2, r_*
nodes.statement:
Let $r_1,q_2,r_*$ be defined as the unique zeros
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  0&=\mathrm H_2(r_1)-\Bigl(\frac53\log_25-2\Bigr)r_1
      -\log_23-\frac43+\frac{10}{9}\log_25,\\
   &\qquad r_1\in(\tfrac14,\tfrac13),\\
  0&=2\mathrm I(q_2)+\mathrm I(1-2q_2)+2q_2-\log_23-\frac59\log_25+\frac23,\\
   &\qquad q_2\in(\tfrac25,\tfrac12),\\
  0&=\mathrm H_2(r_*)+\Bigl(5-\frac53\log_25\Bigr)r_*-\frac52+\frac56\log_25,\\
   &\qquad r_*\in(0,\tfrac16).
  \end{aligned}
\]
nodes.statement_short: $r_1,q_2,r_*$ are the unique zeros of three explicit entropy equations on given intervals.

nodes.name: Switching constants b_1, b_2, p^*
nodes.statement:
Then the three switching constants are
\[
  b_1=\frac{1-2r_1}{2(1-r_1)},\qquad
  b_2=\frac{q_2}{1+q_2},\qquad
  p^*=\frac{1-3r_*}{2-3r_*}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Switching points $b_1,b_2,p^*$ as rational functions of $r_1,q_2,r_*$.

nodes.name: Crossing equations as zero equations
nodes.statement:
The substitutions
$r=(\tfrac12-x)/(1-x)$, $q=x/(1-x)$, and
$r=(1-2x)/(3(1-x))$ convert respectively $\Pi=\Theta$, $\Theta=N$, and
$W_{\mathrm{iso}}=F_\ell$ into these zero equations.
conclusions:
convert respectively $\Pi=\Theta$, $\Theta=N$, and
$W_{\mathrm{iso}}=F_\ell$ into these zero equations
nodes.statement_short: Substitutions turn the crossing conditions $\Pi=\Theta$, $\Theta=N$, $W_{iso}=F_\ell$ into the zero equations defining $r_1,q_2,r_*$.

nodes.name: Main theorem (seven-piece redundancy envelope for Shannon--Fano codes)
nodes.statement:
For every source with $n\ge2$ symbols,
\[
   \boxed{\ \ R\ <\ \begin{cases}
   p_1+C, & 0<p_1<\tfrac14,\\[2pt]
   \Pi(p_1), & \tfrac14\le p_1\le b_1,\\[2pt]
   \Theta(p_1), & b_1\le p_1\le b_2,\\[2pt]
   N(p_1), & b_2\le p_1<\tfrac13,\\[2pt]
   W_{\mathrm{iso}}(p_1), & \tfrac13\le p_1\le p^*,\\[2pt]
   F_\ell(p_1), & p^*\le p_1<\tfrac12,\\[2pt]
   V(p_1), & \tfrac12\le p_1<1,
   \end{cases}\ \ }
\]
with the curves $\Pi,\Theta,N,W_{\mathrm{iso}},F_\ell,V$ and the switching
points $b_1<b_2$, $p^*$ as defined above.
Consequently $R<K=\tfrac52-\tfrac56\log_25$ for every source with
$p_1<\tfrac12$.

   W_{\mathrm{iso}}(p_1), & \tfrac13\le p_1\le p^*,\\[2pt]

nodes.statement_short: Redundancy of binary Shannon--Fano coding is below a seven-piece function $f(p_1)$ of the largest probability; in particular $R<K\approx0.5651$ when $p_1<1/2$.

nodes.name: Tightness of the envelope
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(a)}] For every $p_1\in[\tfrac12,1)$,
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
    &\sup\{R(p):p\text{ a source with largest symbol }p_1\}\\
    &\qquad\qquad=2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1);
  \end{aligned}
  \]
  the supremum is approached but not attained. The final branch of
  Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is therefore best possible.
\item[\textup{(b)}] $R<1$ for every source, and the supremum of $R$ over all
  sources equals $1$, i.e.\ $\sup_{p} R(p)=1$; so no constant bound smaller than
  $1$ is possible, and the branches (each $<1$, the final $\to1$ as $p_1\to1$)
  are consistent with this.
\item[\textup{(c)}] On $[b_2,\tfrac13)$ the $N$ branch is the exact
  supremum of $R$ given $p_1$, approached but not attained
  (Proposition~\ref{prop:tight-q}).
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Where the bound is tight
nodes.statement:
The branch $2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$ is the exact supremum for every $p_1\ge\tfrac12$
(Proposition~\ref{prop:tight}(a)), and $R<1$ is sharp over all sources. In the
potential form (Theorem~\ref{thm:aff}) both parameters are pinned: the
coefficient $\lambda=1+5\kappa(\tfrac15)$ is the least the shape-$(3,3)$ argument
admits ($\sup_{0<t\le1/5}\kappa(t)/t=\lambda-1$ exactly,
Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(ii)), and, given $\lambda$, the constant
$C=\psi(\tfrac13)=c_3+\tfrac{\lambda-1}3$ is the smallest for
which the induction closes, with equality exactly at the uniform ternary
source; the same critical value $\beta=-1-\log_23+\tfrac{10}9\log_25$ appears as
the maximum of Case A and as $F(W_1)$ in Case B2, at the same balanced
configuration $p_1=p_2=\tfrac13$.
nodes.statement_short: Both constants $\lambda$ and $C$ of the potential are pinned, and the $p_1\ge1/2$ branch and $R<1$ are sharp.
nodes.label: rem:where

nodes.name: A simpler proof of a weaker constant
nodes.statement:
If one bounds the $(1,3)$ shape by the induction hypothesis alone, without
expanding the recursion a further step, the same case analysis closes with the cruder coefficient
$\tfrac65$ in place of $\lambda$ (justified by the quadratic bound of
Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(i): in shape $(3,3)$,
$E\le(2a-1)^2\le p_k^2\le\tfrac15p_k$) and the constant
$3c_3=5-3\log_23=0.2451\ldots$ in place of $C$: the $(1,3)$ requirement
becomes $1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\le3c_3\,p_1$ on $[\tfrac13,\tfrac12)$, which holds by
concavity with equality at $p_1=\tfrac13$.
nodes.statement_short: Without expanding the $(1,3)$ shape, the induction closes with coefficient $6/5$ and constant $3c_3$.
nodes.label: rem:simple

nodes.name: Limits of the method
nodes.statement:
The affine constant $C$ is not the least slope-one excess. The worst sources
for $R-p_1$ are near-uniform: several equal leading symbols followed by a long
near-uniform tail, for which the redundancy splits as an algebraic term plus
(tail mass) times the redundancy of the uniform tail, whose supremum over the
tail size is the fluctuation constant $\sigma=1-\log_2 e+\log_2\log_2 e$ of
uniform-source redundancy. Pushing the slope-one constant to its true value
would therefore require bounding the redundancy of the near-uniform blocks in
the recursion by $\sigma$-type constants; for Huffman codes this is exactly what
the sibling property provides \cite{Gallager78}, and Fano codes lack it. All
techniques here are sibling-free. Within the present min-corrected induction the
two constants are pinned: the uniform ternary source forces
$C=c_3+(\lambda-1)/3$, and the shape-$(3,3)$ argument forces
$\lambda-1\ge\sup_{0<t\le1/5}\kappa(t)/t=5\kappa(\tfrac15)$, both attained; the $(3,3)$
equality geometry ($a=\tfrac35$, three left symbols of mass $\tfrac15$) is the
four-equal-leader configuration at $p_1=\tfrac15$ against which $\lambda$ is tight.
Any further improvement must break the uniform-ternary binding itself, for
instance by an exact treatment of three-symbol blocks in place of the induction
hypothesis, rather than by sharpening the scalar estimates.
nodes.statement_short: $C$ is not optimal; near-uniform sources need sibling-type control that Fano codes lack.
nodes.label: rem:limits

nodes.name: Recursion and node sum (Fano recursion)
nodes.statement:
If the root splits into a left part of mass $a$ and right part of mass $1-a$,
with renormalised sub-sources $B_L,B_R$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R\ &=\ \bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(a)\bigr)+a\,R(B_L)+(1-a)\,R(B_R),\\
  1-\mathrm H_2(a)&=\kappa(2a-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Iterating: $R=\sum_{v}M_v\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(a_v)\bigr)$, the sum over internal nodes
$v$, where $M_v$ is the global mass of the block at $v$ and $a_v$ is its
left-mass fraction.
assumptions:
the root splits into a left part of mass $a$ and right part of mass $1-a$,
with renormalised sub-sources $B_L,B_R$
conclusions:
Iterating: $R=\sum_{v}M_v\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(a_v)\bigr)$, the sum over internal nodes
$v$, where $M_v$ is the global mass of the block at $v$ and $a_v$ is its
left-mass fraction

nodes.label: lem:rec

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement:
Every symbol in a part is one level deeper than in the renormalised sub-source, so
$L=1+a\,L(B_L)+(1-a)\,L(B_R)$. The entropy grouping rule gives
$\mathrm H=\mathrm H_2(a)+a\,\mathrm H(B_L)+(1-a)\,\mathrm H(B_R)$. Subtract, and telescope down the tree
(leaves contribute $0$).
nodes.statement_short: Expected length and entropy both satisfy the grouping recursion; subtract and telescope.

nodes.name: Length recursion
nodes.statement:
Every symbol in a part is one level deeper than in the renormalised sub-source, so
$L=1+a\,L(B_L)+(1-a)\,L(B_R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each symbol in a part is one level deeper, giving the length recursion.

nodes.name: Entropy grouping
nodes.statement:
The entropy grouping rule gives
$\mathrm H=\mathrm H_2(a)+a\,\mathrm H(B_L)+(1-a)\,\mathrm H(B_R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the entropy grouping rule.

nodes.name: Subtract and telescope
nodes.statement:
Subtract, and telescope down the tree
(leaves contribute $0$).
nodes.statement_short: Subtract and telescope down the tree.

nodes.name: Chord, quadratic, and ratio bounds for kappa
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] For $d\in[-1,1]$,
\[
  \kappa(d)\le|d|,\qquad \kappa(d)\le d^2 .
\]
\item[\textup{(ii)}] $\kappa$ is strictly convex on $[-1,1]$ and strictly
increasing on $[0,1]$, and the ratio $\kappa(t)/t$ is strictly increasing on
$(0,1]$; consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &\kappa(t)\ \le\ 5\,\kappa(\tfrac15)\,t\ =\ (\lambda-1)\,t
  \quad\text{on }[0,\tfrac15],\\
  &\text{with equality iff }t\in\{0,\tfrac15\},
\end{aligned}
\]
and $\lambda-1=\sup_{0<t\le1/5}\kappa(t)/t$ exactly.
\end{enumerate}
conclusions:
$\kappa$ is strictly convex on $[-1,1]$ and strictly
increasing on $[0,1]$
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(d)\le\min(|d|,d^2)$; $\kappa(t)/t$ increases, so $\kappa(t)\le(\lambda-1)t$ on $[0,1/5]$ with $\lambda-1$ optimal.
nodes.label: lem:kappa

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
(i) $\kappa$ is convex and even with $\kappa(0)=0$ and $\kappa(1)=1$. A convex function
lies below the \emph{chord} joining any two points of its graph, so on $[0,1]$
the graph of $\kappa$ lies below the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$; this gives
$\kappa(d)\le(1-d)\kappa(0)+d\kappa(1)=d$, and evenness extends it to $\kappa(d)\le|d|$. We
refer to this estimate as the \emph{chord bound}. The
quadratic bound follows from the Taylor expansion
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathrm H_2\Bigl(\tfrac{1+d}{2}\Bigr)\ &=\ 1-\frac{1}{\ln2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{d^{2k}}{2k(2k-1)},\\
  \text{i.e.}\quad
  \kappa(d)\ &=\ \frac{1}{\ln2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{d^{2k}}{2k(2k-1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $d^{2k}\le d^2$ for $|d|\le1$ and
$\sum_{k\ge1}\tfrac1{2k(2k-1)}=\sum_{k\ge1}\bigl(\tfrac1{2k-1}-\tfrac1{2k}\bigr)
=1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\cdots=\ln2$ (the alternating harmonic series), it follows
that $\kappa(d)\le\tfrac{d^2}{\ln2}\cdot\ln2=d^2$.

(ii) $\mathrm H_2''(x)=-\tfrac1{x(1-x)\ln2}<0$ makes $\mathrm H_2$ strictly concave, hence
$\kappa$ strictly convex (affine inner map). For $0<s<t\le1$, writing
$s=\tfrac st\,t+(1-\tfrac st)\cdot0$, strict convexity and $\kappa(0)=0$ give
$\kappa(s)<\tfrac st\,\kappa(t)$, i.e.\ $\kappa(s)/s<\kappa(t)/t$: the ratio is strictly
increasing, and since $\kappa(t)>0$ for $t>0$ the same display shows that $\kappa$
is strictly increasing on $[0,1]$. The stated bound is the ratio at
$t=\tfrac15$, using $\kappa(\tfrac15)=(\lambda-1)/5$, the definition
\eqref{eq:constants} of $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Chord bound from convexity, quadratic bound from the Taylor series of $\mathrm H_2$; ratio monotonicity from strict convexity.

nodes.name: Part (i): chord and quadratic bounds
nodes.statement:
(i) $\kappa$ is convex and even with $\kappa(0)=0$ and $\kappa(1)=1$. A convex function
lies below the \emph{chord} joining any two points of its graph, so on $[0,1]$
the graph of $\kappa$ lies below the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$; this gives
$\kappa(d)\le(1-d)\kappa(0)+d\kappa(1)=d$, and evenness extends it to $\kappa(d)\le|d|$. We
refer to this estimate as the \emph{chord bound}. The
quadratic bound follows from the Taylor expansion
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathrm H_2\Bigl(\tfrac{1+d}{2}\Bigr)\ &=\ 1-\frac{1}{\ln2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{d^{2k}}{2k(2k-1)},\\
  \text{i.e.}\quad
  \kappa(d)\ &=\ \frac{1}{\ln2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{d^{2k}}{2k(2k-1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $d^{2k}\le d^2$ for $|d|\le1$ and
$\sum_{k\ge1}\tfrac1{2k(2k-1)}=\sum_{k\ge1}\bigl(\tfrac1{2k-1}-\tfrac1{2k}\bigr)
=1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\cdots=\ln2$ (the alternating harmonic series), it follows
that $\kappa(d)\le\tfrac{d^2}{\ln2}\cdot\ln2=d^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Chord bound by convexity; quadratic bound via Taylor expansion and the alternating harmonic series.

nodes.name: Part (ii): strict convexity and ratio
nodes.statement:
(ii) $\mathrm H_2''(x)=-\tfrac1{x(1-x)\ln2}<0$ makes $\mathrm H_2$ strictly concave, hence
$\kappa$ strictly convex (affine inner map). For $0<s<t\le1$, writing
$s=\tfrac st\,t+(1-\tfrac st)\cdot0$, strict convexity and $\kappa(0)=0$ give
$\kappa(s)<\tfrac st\,\kappa(t)$, i.e.\ $\kappa(s)/s<\kappa(t)/t$: the ratio is strictly
increasing, and since $\kappa(t)>0$ for $t>0$ the same display shows that $\kappa$
is strictly increasing on $[0,1]$. The stated bound is the ratio at
$t=\tfrac15$, using $\kappa(\tfrac15)=(\lambda-1)/5$, the definition
\eqref{eq:constants} of $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Strict concavity of $\mathrm H_2$ gives strict convexity and an increasing ratio $\kappa(t)/t$.

nodes.name: Key lemma: imbalance at most least left symbol
nodes.statement:
At every internal node, the chosen split satisfies $|m_L-m_R|\le p_k$, where
$p_k$ is the last \textup{(}least\textup{)} symbol of the left part. Moreover, when
$m_L<m_R$ one has $m_R-m_L\le p_{k+1}$, the first symbol of the right part.
nodes.statement_short: A Fano split's imbalance is at most the least symbol of the left part (and at most the first right symbol when the left is lighter).
nodes.label: lem:key

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement:
Let the cut be after position $k$ and $x=m_L-m_R$. If $x\ge0$ and the left part
is a singleton, then $x=2p_k-M\le p_k$ directly ($M$, the block mass, is
$\ge p_k$). Otherwise, for $x\ge0$, moving the cut one
step left transfers $p_k$ to the right and yields imbalance $|x-2p_k|$;
optimality of the cut gives $x\le|x-2p_k|$. If $x>2p_k$ this reads
$x\le x-2p_k$, impossible; hence $x\le2p_k$ and then $x\le2p_k-x$, i.e.\
$x\le p_k$. If $x<0$: were the right part a single symbol, the left part would
contain at least one symbol $\ge$ that symbol, giving $x\ge0$; so the cut can move
one step right, transferring $p_{k+1}$, and the same argument gives
$-x\le p_{k+1}\le p_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the sign of the imbalance, comparing with the cut moved one step by optimality.

nodes.name: Singleton left part
nodes.statement:
Let the cut be after position $k$ and $x=m_L-m_R$. If $x\ge0$ and the left part
is a singleton, then $x=2p_k-M\le p_k$ directly ($M$, the block mass, is
$\ge p_k$).
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the imbalance $x$; a singleton left part with $x\ge0$ gives $x\le p_k$ directly.

nodes.name: Nonnegative imbalance
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, for $x\ge0$, moving the cut one
step left transfers $p_k$ to the right and yields imbalance $|x-2p_k|$;
optimality of the cut gives $x\le|x-2p_k|$. If $x>2p_k$ this reads
$x\le x-2p_k$, impossible; hence $x\le2p_k$ and then $x\le2p_k-x$, i.e.\
$x\le p_k$.
nodes.statement_short: For $x\ge0$, optimality against moving the cut left gives $x\le p_k$.

nodes.name: Negative imbalance
nodes.statement:
If $x<0$: were the right part a single symbol, the left part would
contain at least one symbol $\ge$ that symbol, giving $x\ge0$; so the cut can move
one step right, transferring $p_{k+1}$, and the same argument gives
$-x\le p_{k+1}\le p_k$.
nodes.statement_short: For $x<0$, moving the cut right gives $-x\le p_{k+1}\le p_k$.

nodes.name: Krajci--Liu--Mikes--Moser universal bound
nodes.statement:
For the Shannon--Fano/Fano splitting code,
\[
  R\le1-p_n .
\]
In particular $R<1$ for every finite source.
nodes.label: lem:univ

nodes.name: Isolation criterion and reduction
nodes.statement:
The root splits the leader off alone \textup{(}left part $=\{1\}$\textup{)} iff
$2p_1+p_2\ge1$; in particular this holds whenever $p_1\ge\tfrac12$, and it forces
$p_1\ge\tfrac13$. In that case
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R\ &=\ \bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(1-p_1)\,R(\rho),\\
  \rho&=\tfrac{1}{1-p_1}\,(p_2,\dots,p_n).
\end{aligned}
\]
conclusions:
The root splits the leader off alone \textup{(}left part $=\{1\}$\textup{)} iff
$2p_1+p_2\ge1$
equivalent_conditions: The root splits the leader off alone
nodes.statement_short: The root isolates the leader iff $2p_1+p_2\ge1$ (forcing $p_1\ge1/3$), and then $R=1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)+(1-p_1)R(\rho)$.
nodes.label: lem:iso

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement:
As the cut moves right the signed imbalance $2(\text{prefix mass})-1$ strictly
increases. The cut after position $1$ is at least as good as the cut after position $2$ iff
$|2p_1-1|\le|2(p_1+p_2)-1|$, which simplifies (in both sign cases) to
$2p_1+p_2\ge1$; and when this holds, the signed imbalance at position $2$ is
already $2p_1+2p_2-1\ge p_2\ge0$, so all later cuts are worse. Conversely, if
$2p_1+p_2<1$ the cut after position~$2$ is strictly better than after
position~$1$. With $p_2\le p_1$, $2p_1+p_2\ge1$ forces $3p_1\ge1$. The identity
is Lemma~\ref{lem:rec} with $a=p_1$ and $R(B_L)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The signed imbalance increases along the cuts; compare the first two cuts, then apply the recursion with $a=p_1$.

nodes.name: Compare first two cuts
nodes.statement:
As the cut moves right the signed imbalance $2(\text{prefix mass})-1$ strictly
increases. The cut after position $1$ is at least as good as the cut after position $2$ iff
$|2p_1-1|\le|2(p_1+p_2)-1|$, which simplifies (in both sign cases) to
$2p_1+p_2\ge1$; and when this holds, the signed imbalance at position $2$ is
already $2p_1+2p_2-1\ge p_2\ge0$, so all later cuts are worse.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone signed imbalance: cut 1 is optimal iff $2p_1+p_2\ge1$.

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement:
Conversely, if
$2p_1+p_2<1$ the cut after position~$2$ is strictly better than after
position~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: If $2p_1+p_2<1$ the second cut is strictly better.

nodes.name: Lower bound on p_1
nodes.statement: With $p_2\le p_1$, $2p_1+p_2\ge1$ forces $3p_1\ge1$.
nodes.statement_short: With $p_2\le p_1$, isolation forces $3p_1\ge1$.

nodes.name: Reduction identity
nodes.statement:
The identity
is Lemma~\ref{lem:rec} with $a=p_1$ and $R(B_L)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The identity is Lemma 1 with $a=p_1$.

nodes.name: Isolation ceiling
nodes.statement:
If $2p_1+p_2\ge1$ \textup{(}in particular if $p_1\ge\tfrac12$\textup{)}, then
$R<2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$. More generally, for any block in which the most probable symbol is split off on its own, the
redundancy is less than $2-\beta-\mathrm H_2(\beta)$, where $\beta$ is that
symbol's fraction of the block mass.
assumptions: for any block in which the most probable symbol is split off on its own
for any block in which the most probable symbol is split off on its own

nodes.statement_short: When the leader is isolated, $R<V(p_1)=2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$; likewise for any block with its leader split off.
nodes.label: cor:isob

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{lem:iso} and $R(\rho)<1$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:univ}) give
$R<(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1))+(1-p_1)$; the block form is the same computation after
renormalisation.
nodes.statement_short: Plug the universal bound $R(\rho)<1$ into the isolation reduction.

nodes.name: Proof of the final branch of the Main Theorem
nodes.statement: The final branch of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is Corollary~\ref{cor:isob}.
nodes.statement_short: The $p_1\ge1/2$ branch of the main theorem is the isolation ceiling.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1(a)
nodes.statement:
The upper bound is Corollary~\ref{cor:isob}. For the lower bound fix
$p_1\in[\tfrac12,1)$ and $q\in[\tfrac12,1)$, and consider the three-symbol source
\[
  p\ =\ \bigl(p_1,\ (1-p_1)q,\ (1-p_1)(1-q)\bigr),
\]
which is sorted since $(1-p_1)q\le p_1$ for $p_1\ge\tfrac12$. Since $2p_1\ge1$
the root splits the leader off on its own (Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}), and the remaining binary block has
redundancy $1-\mathrm H_2(q)$. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R&=\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(1-p_1)\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(q)\bigr)\\
  &\ \xrightarrow[q\to1^-]{}\ 2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1).
\end{aligned}
\]
The supremum is not attained because $R<2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$ always
(Corollary~\ref{cor:isob}).
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from the isolation ceiling; lower bound by a three-symbol family with $q\to1$.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: The upper bound is Corollary~\ref{cor:isob}.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound is Corollary 1.

nodes.name: Extremal family
nodes.statement:
For the lower bound fix
$p_1\in[\tfrac12,1)$ and $q\in[\tfrac12,1)$, and consider the three-symbol source
\[
  p\ =\ \bigl(p_1,\ (1-p_1)q,\ (1-p_1)(1-q)\bigr),
\]
which is sorted since $(1-p_1)q\le p_1$ for $p_1\ge\tfrac12$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider the sorted three-symbol source $(p_1,(1-p_1)q,(1-p_1)(1-q))$.

nodes.name: Compute its redundancy
nodes.statement:
Since $2p_1\ge1$
the root splits the leader off on its own (Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}), and the remaining binary block has
redundancy $1-\mathrm H_2(q)$. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R&=\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(1-p_1)\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(q)\bigr)\\
  &\ \xrightarrow[q\to1^-]{}\ 2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.statement_short: Leader is isolated; $R\to2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$ as $q\to1$.

nodes.name: Not attained
nodes.statement:
The supremum is not attained because $R<2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$ always
(Corollary~\ref{cor:isob}).
nodes.statement_short: The strict bound of Corollary 1 shows the supremum is not attained.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1(b)
nodes.statement:
$R<1$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:univ}. For the supremum, the binary source
$(1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ has $R=1-\mathrm H_2(\varepsilon)\to1$ as
$\varepsilon\to0^+$.
nodes.statement_short: $R<1$ by the universal bound; binary sources $(1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ approach 1.

nodes.name: Isolation ceiling applies below 1/2
nodes.statement:
Corollary~\ref{cor:isob} bounds $R$ by $2-p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$ whenever $2p_1+p_2\ge1$,
i.e.\ also for a range of sources with $p_1\in[\tfrac13,\tfrac12)$. Only the
condition on $(p_1,p_2)$, not $p_1\ge\tfrac12$ itself, is used.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 1 only uses $2p_1+p_2\ge1$, so it also covers some sources with $p_1<1/2$.

nodes.name: Potential form (affine potential bound)
nodes.statement:
For every source with $n\ge3$ symbols,
\[
  R\ \le\ \Psi(p)\ :=\ p_1+C-\lambda\,p_n ,
\]
with equality iff $p=(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$.
nodes.statement_short: $R\le p_1+C-\lambda p_n$ for $n\ge3$, with equality only for the uniform ternary source.
nodes.label: thm:aff

nodes.name: Affine bound R < p_1 + C
nodes.label: cor:aff

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement:
For $n\ge3$, Theorem~\ref{thm:aff} gives $R\le p_1+C-\lambda p_n<p_1+C$
since $\lambda,p_n>0$. For $n=2$ (where necessarily $p_1\ge\tfrac12$), the chord
bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}) gives $R=\kappa(2p_1-1)\le2p_1-1<p_1<p_1+C$.
nodes.statement_short: Drop the positive $\lambda p_n$ term for $n\ge3$; use the chord bound for $n=2$.

nodes.name: Shape of the root split
nodes.statement:
The root split cuts the sorted list $p_1\ge\cdots\ge p_n$ into a left part,
which contains the leader $p_1$, and a right part. We record its
\emph{shape} as the ordered pair of these two part sizes, with any size of
three or more written simply as $3$. Thus shape $(1,2)$ means the leader
sits alone on the left with exactly two symbols on the right; $(1,3)$ means
the leader alone on the left with three or more symbols on the right; and
$(3,3)$ means at least three symbols on each side.
nodes.statement_short: Shape = ordered pair of left/right part sizes at the root, sizes $\ge3$ written as 3.

nodes.name: Shapes of the root split
nodes.statement:
Let $p_1<\tfrac12$ and $n\ge3$. Then the shape of the root split is one of
\[
  (1,2),\quad(1,3),\quad(2,2),\quad(2,3),\quad(3,3),
\]
unless the source is uniform with $n\in\{3,5\}$ \textup{(}handled separately in
\S\ref{ss:unif}\textup{)}. Moreover a split of shape $(1,\cdot)$ satisfies
$2p_1+p_2\ge1$, hence $p_1\ge\tfrac13$; a split of shape $(2,\cdot)$ or
$(3,\cdot)$ \textup{(}a \emph{group} split\textup{)} satisfies $2p_1+p_2<1$,
and the mass $a$ of its left part obeys $a<\tfrac23$; a group split of shape $(2,\cdot)$ has
$a\ge\tfrac25$.
conclusions:
a split of shape $(1,\cdot)$ satisfies
$2p_1+p_2\ge1$, hence $p_1\ge\tfrac13$
the mass $a$ of its left part obeys $a<\tfrac23$

a group split of shape $(2,\cdot)$ has
$a\ge\tfrac25$
nodes.statement_short: For $p_1<1/2$ the root shape is one of $(1,2),(1,3),(2,2),(2,3),(3,3)$ except uniform $n\in\{3,5\}$; group splits have $a<2/3$.
nodes.label: lem:shapes

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement:
The isolate/group dichotomy and $p_1\ge\tfrac13$ are Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}. For a
group split, $p_1\ge p_2$ gives $\tfrac32a\le\tfrac32(p_1+p_2)\le2p_1+p_2<1$,
so $a<\tfrac23$. For shape $(2,\cdot)$: if $a\ge\tfrac12$ then $a\ge\tfrac25$
trivially; if $a<\tfrac12$, Lemma~\ref{lem:key} gives $1-2a=|2a-1|\le p_2$,
while $p_2\le\tfrac a2$ (as $p_1\ge p_2$, $p_1+p_2=a$), so $1\le\tfrac52a$. It remains to exclude shapes with right part of size $1$, and shape $(3,2)$.

\textbf{Right part of size $1$} (cut after $n-1$): the imbalance is $1-2p_n$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:key} gives $1-2p_n\le p_{n-1}\le p_1<\tfrac12$, so
$p_n>\tfrac14$. For $n\ge4$ all symbols then exceed $\tfrac14$ and the total mass
exceeds $1$, a contradiction. For $n=3$, cutting after position $1$ (imbalance
$1-2p_1$) is at least as good as after position $2$ (imbalance $1-2p_3\ge1-2p_1$),
with equality only if $p_1=p_3$, i.e.\ the uniform ternary source.

\textbf{Shape $(3,2)$} (cut after $n-2$, $n\ge5$): let $s=p_{n-1}+p_n$. If
$s\ge\tfrac12$ then $p_{n-1}\ge\tfrac s2\ge\tfrac14$, so all symbols exceed
$\tfrac14$ and again the mass exceeds $1$; hence $s<\tfrac12$ and the imbalance
is $1-2s>0$. Moving the cut one step left transfers $p_{n-2}$ and produces
signed imbalance $1-2s-2p_{n-2}$; optimality requires
$1-2s\le|1-2s-2p_{n-2}|$, which forces $1-2s-2p_{n-2}<0$ and
\begin{equation} p_{n-2}+2p_{n-1}+2p_n\ \ge\ 1 .
\end{equation}
On the other hand the $n-2$ largest symbols are each $\ge p_{n-2}$, so
\begin{equation} (n-2)\,p_{n-2}+p_{n-1}+p_n\ \le\ 1 .
\end{equation}
Subtracting \eqref{eq:32a} from \eqref{eq:32b}:
$(n-3)p_{n-2}\le p_{n-1}+p_n\le2p_{n-2}$, hence $n\le5$. For $n=5$ all the
inequalities are forced into equalities, giving $p_1=\cdots=p_5=\tfrac15$, the
uniform quinary source.
nodes.statement_short: Isolation criterion plus the key lemma bound the left mass; right singletons and shape $(3,2)$ are excluded by mass counting.

nodes.name: Dichotomy and group mass
nodes.statement:
The isolate/group dichotomy and $p_1\ge\tfrac13$ are Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}. For a
group split, $p_1\ge p_2$ gives $\tfrac32a\le\tfrac32(p_1+p_2)\le2p_1+p_2<1$,
so $a<\tfrac23$.
nodes.statement_short: Isolation criterion gives the dichotomy; group splits have $a<2/3$.

nodes.name: Shape (2,.) mass bound
nodes.statement:
For shape $(2,\cdot)$: if $a\ge\tfrac12$ then $a\ge\tfrac25$
trivially; if $a<\tfrac12$, Lemma~\ref{lem:key} gives $1-2a=|2a-1|\le p_2$,
while $p_2\le\tfrac a2$ (as $p_1\ge p_2$, $p_1+p_2=a$), so $1\le\tfrac52a$.
nodes.statement_short: Key lemma gives $a\ge2/5$ for shape $(2,\cdot)$.

nodes.name: Remaining exclusions
nodes.statement: It remains to exclude shapes with right part of size $1$, and shape $(3,2)$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to exclude right singletons and shape $(3,2)$.

nodes.name: Right part of size 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Right part of size $1$} (cut after $n-1$): the imbalance is $1-2p_n$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:key} gives $1-2p_n\le p_{n-1}\le p_1<\tfrac12$, so
$p_n>\tfrac14$. For $n\ge4$ all symbols then exceed $\tfrac14$ and the total mass
exceeds $1$, a contradiction. For $n=3$, cutting after position $1$ (imbalance
$1-2p_1$) is at least as good as after position $2$ (imbalance $1-2p_3\ge1-2p_1$),
with equality only if $p_1=p_3$, i.e.\ the uniform ternary source.
nodes.statement_short: A right singleton forces all symbols $>1/4$; only the uniform ternary source survives.

nodes.name: Shape (3,2)
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Shape $(3,2)$} (cut after $n-2$, $n\ge5$): let $s=p_{n-1}+p_n$. If
$s\ge\tfrac12$ then $p_{n-1}\ge\tfrac s2\ge\tfrac14$, so all symbols exceed
$\tfrac14$ and again the mass exceeds $1$; hence $s<\tfrac12$ and the imbalance
is $1-2s>0$. Moving the cut one step left transfers $p_{n-2}$ and produces
signed imbalance $1-2s-2p_{n-2}$; optimality requires
$1-2s\le|1-2s-2p_{n-2}|$, which forces $1-2s-2p_{n-2}<0$ and
\begin{equation} p_{n-2}+2p_{n-1}+2p_n\ \ge\ 1 .
\end{equation}
On the other hand the $n-2$ largest symbols are each $\ge p_{n-2}$, so
\begin{equation} (n-2)\,p_{n-2}+p_{n-1}+p_n\ \le\ 1 .
\end{equation}
Subtracting \eqref{eq:32a} from \eqref{eq:32b}:
$(n-3)p_{n-2}\le p_{n-1}+p_n\le2p_{n-2}$, hence $n\le5$. For $n=5$ all the
inequalities are forced into equalities, giving $p_1=\cdots=p_5=\tfrac15$, the
uniform quinary source.
nodes.statement_short: Optimality and sorting force $n\le5$, and $n=5$ only for the uniform quinary source.

nodes.name: Entropy of affine arguments is concave
nodes.statement:
Throughout we use the standing observation that the entropy
$\mathrm H(a_1(t),\dots,a_k(t))$ of affine arguments is a concave
function of $t$ (each $\mathrm I$ is concave), so that subtractive
affine and entropy expressions are convex and are maximised at endpoints of
intervals.
also_stated_at:
We use repeatedly that a sum of an affine function and terms
$-\mathrm I(u(\cdot))$ with $u$ affine is convex (each term contributes
$+c^2/(u\ln2)$ to the second derivative, where $c$ is the slope of $u$) and attains
its maximum over an interval at an endpoint.
nodes.statement_short: Entropy of affinely parametrised arguments is concave, so affine-minus-entropy expressions are convex and maximised at interval endpoints.

nodes.name: Scalar inequalities S1-S3
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(S1)}] $\psi(x):=1-\mathrm H_2(x)+(\lambda-1)(1-2x)$ is strictly
decreasing on $[\tfrac13,\tfrac12]$, and
$\psi(\tfrac13)=c_3+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{3}=C$.
\item[\textup{(S2)}] $h(x):=\bigl(2-2x-\mathrm H_2(x)\bigr)+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-x)
\ \le\ \tfrac{\lambda-1}{4}$ on $[\tfrac12,1]$, and $\tfrac{\lambda-1}4<C$.
\item[\textup{(S3)}] \textup{(chord)} $1-\mathrm H_2(a)\ \le\ 6c_3\,(a-\tfrac12)$ on
$[\tfrac12,\tfrac23]$.
\end{enumerate}
conclusions:
$\psi(x):=1-\mathrm H_2(x)+(\lambda-1)(1-2x)$ is strictly
decreasing on $[\tfrac13,\tfrac12]$, and
$\psi(\tfrac13)=c_3+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{3}=C$
nodes.statement_short: Three scalar facts: $\psi$ decreases with $\psi(1/3)=C$; $h\le(\lambda-1)/4<C$ on $[1/2,1]$; chord bound $1-\mathrm H_2(a)\le6c_3(a-1/2)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement:
(S1) $\psi'(x)=-\mathrm H_2'(x)-2(\lambda-1)=\log_2\tfrac{x}{1-x}-2(\lambda-1)<0$ for
$x\le\tfrac12$ (the logarithm is $\le0$ there and $\lambda>1$), and
$\psi(\tfrac13)=c_3+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{3}$, which is the definition
\eqref{eq:constants} of $C$; by \eqref{eq:cancel} the $\log_23$-terms cancel
and $C=4-\tfrac53\log_25$.

(S2) $h$ is convex ($-\mathrm H_2$ convex plus affine), so its maximum on $[\tfrac12,1]$
is at an endpoint: $h(\tfrac12)=0+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{4}$ and $h(1)=0$. And
$\tfrac{\lambda-1}4<\tfrac{\lambda-1}2<C$.

(S3) $1-\mathrm H_2$ is convex, hence lies below its chord on $[\tfrac12,\tfrac23]$
through $\bigl(\tfrac12,0\bigr)$ and $\bigl(\tfrac23,1-\mathrm H_2(\tfrac23)\bigr)$;
and $\mathrm H_2(\tfrac23)=\mathrm H_2(\tfrac13)$, so the chord's slope is
$c_3/\tfrac16=6c_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Derivative sign for (S1), convexity with endpoint evaluation for (S2), chord of a convex function for (S3).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2: induction and the shapes
nodes.statement:
We prove Theorem~\ref{thm:aff} by strong induction on $n$: the full
statement (the inequality together with its equality clause) is
assumed for all sources with $3\le n'<n$ symbols (IH). In the recursion
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rec}) a part $S$ with symbols $p_i\ge\cdots\ge p_j$ and mass $w$
contributes $w\,R(B_S)$, which we bound by
\begin{equation} w\,R(B_S)\ \le\
  \begin{cases}
    0,\\
    \quad |S|=1,\\[2pt]
    p_i-p_j,\\
    \quad |S|=2\quad(\text{chord: }w\,\kappa\bigl(\tfrac{p_i-p_j}{w}\bigr)\\
    \qquad\quad\le p_i-p_j),\\[2pt]
    p_i+w\,C-\lambda\,p_j,\\
    \quad |S|\ge3\quad(\text{IH}),
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
the middle bound with equality iff $p_i=p_j$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(i);
$\tfrac{p_i-p_j}{w}=1$ is impossible as $p_j>0$), the last with equality iff
$B_S$ is uniform ternary (the IH's equality clause). Let the root split have
left mass $a$ and set $E:=1-\mathrm H_2(a)=\kappa(2a-1)$. By
Lemmas~\ref{lem:kappa} and~\ref{lem:key},
\begin{equation} E\ \le\ |2a-1|\ \le\ p_k
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  E\ \le\ (2a-1)^2 ,
\end{equation}
$p_k$ being the least symbol of the left part. Writing $\Phi$ for the resulting
upper bound on $R$, it suffices in each case to show $\Phi\le\Psi
=p_1+C-\lambda p_n$, tracking where equality can occur.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Dominant leader ($p_1\ge\tfrac12$).}
The root splits the leader off on its own; the rest $\rho$ has $n-1\ge2$ symbols and least symbol
$\tfrac{p_n}{1-p_1}$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:univ} gives
$R\le(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1))+(1-p_1)-p_n$. Then, using $p_n\le\tfrac12(1-p_1)$ and
$\lambda>1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R-\Psi\ &\le\ \bigl(2-2p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(\lambda-1)p_n-C\\
  &\le\ h(p_1)-C\ \le\ \tfrac{\lambda-1}{4}-C\ <\ 0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (S2).

\smallskip
For $p_1<\tfrac12$ we go through the shapes of Lemma~\ref{lem:shapes}. Shapes
$(1,\cdot)$ have $p_1\in[\tfrac13,\tfrac12)$; group shapes have $a<\tfrac23$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Shape $(1,2)$ (so $n=3$): the binding case.}
Here $\Phi=\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(p_2-p_3)$ and
\[
  \Phi-\Psi=\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+p_2+(\lambda-1)p_3-p_1-C .
\]
Substituting $p_3=1-p_1-p_2$, the middle terms equal
$(2-\lambda)p_2+(\lambda-1)(1-p_1)$, increasing in $p_2$ (since $\lambda<2$); at
the extreme $p_2=p_1$ (so $p_3=1-2p_1$),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Phi-\Psi\ &\le\ \bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(\lambda-1)(1-2p_1)-C\\
  &=\ \psi(p_1)-C\ \le\ \psi(\tfrac13)-C\ =\ 0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (S1). Equality requires
$p_1=\tfrac13$ and $p_2=p_1$ (the $p_2$-coefficient $2-\lambda$ is
positive) and equality in the chord bound for the right part, i.e.\
$p_2=p_3$: the uniform ternary source. This is the extremal case, and it is
what forces the value of the constant, since $C=\psi(\tfrac13)$ is the
smallest for which the bound can hold.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Shape $(2,3)$.}
Here $a=p_1+p_2\in[\tfrac25,\tfrac23)$ and
$\Phi-\Psi=E+(p_1-p_2)+p_3-p_1-a\,C\le E-a\,C$ (since $p_3\le p_2$; the
$\lambda p_n$-terms cancel). On
$[\tfrac25,\tfrac12]$: $E\le(2a-1)^2$ by \eqref{eq:E}, and
$\tfrac{(2a-1)^2}{a}$ has derivative of the sign of $2a-1$, hence is decreasing
there, so $\tfrac Ea\le\tfrac{(1/5)^2}{2/5}<C$. On
$[\tfrac12,\tfrac23)$, (S3) gives
$\tfrac Ea\le6c_3\bigl(1-\tfrac1{2a}\bigr)<\tfrac32c_3<C$. Hence
$E<aC$ and $\Phi<\Psi$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Shape $(2,2)$ (so $n=4$).}
Here $a=p_1+p_2\in[\tfrac25,\tfrac23)$ and
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Phi-\Psi&=E+(p_1-p_2)+(p_3-p_4)-p_1-C+\lambda p_4\\
   &=E-p_2+p_3+(\lambda-1)p_4-C .
\end{aligned}
\]
With $p_3+p_4=1-a$ fixed,
$-p_2+p_3+(\lambda-1)p_4=-p_2+(2-\lambda)p_3+(\lambda-1)(1-a)$
is increasing in $p_3$ ($\lambda<2$), hence maximal at $p_3=p_2$, where it equals
$(\lambda-1)(1-a-p_2)$; and $p_2\ge p_3\ge\tfrac{1-a}{2}$ gives
$(\lambda-1)(1-a-p_2)\le\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)$. Therefore
$\Phi-\Psi\le E+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)-C$. On $[\tfrac25,\tfrac12]$: with
$E\le(2a-1)^2$, the bound $(2a-1)^2+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)$ is convex with
endpoint values $\tfrac1{25}+\tfrac3{10}(\lambda-1)$ at $a=\tfrac25$ and
$\tfrac{\lambda-1}{4}$ at $a=\tfrac12$, and both are less than $C$:
$\tfrac{\lambda-1}4<C$, while
$\tfrac1{25}+\tfrac3{10}(\lambda-1)-C<0$. On $[\tfrac12,\tfrac23)$:
with (S3), $6c_3(a-\tfrac12)+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)$ has positive slope
$6c_3-\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}$, so on $a<\tfrac23$,
\[
  \Phi-\Psi\ <\ 6c_3\cdot\tfrac16+\frac{\lambda-1}{2}\cdot\frac13-C
  <\ 0. 
\]

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Shape $(3,3)$.}
Here the $C$-terms and $p_1,p_n$ cancel and
$\Phi-\Psi=E+p_{k+1}-\lambda p_k$. The left part has at least $3$ symbols of
total mass $a$, so its least symbol obeys $p_k\le\tfrac a3$. If $a\ge\tfrac12$,
then \eqref{eq:E} gives $2a-1\le p_k\le\tfrac a3$, whence $a\le\tfrac35$ and
$p_k\le\tfrac15$; if $a<\tfrac12$ then $p_k\le\tfrac a3<\tfrac15$. In
either case $|2a-1|\le p_k\le\tfrac15$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(ii)
($\kappa$ increasing, then the ratio bound),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  E\ &=\ \kappa(2a-1)\ \le\ \kappa(p_k)\ \le\ (\lambda-1)\,p_k ,\\
  \text{so}\quad
  E+p_{k+1}\ &\le\ (\lambda-1)p_k+p_k\ =\ \lambda\,p_k ,
\end{aligned}
\]
using $p_{k+1}\le p_k$: $\Phi\le\Psi$. This case needs no constant at all,
it is what forces the correction coefficient, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(ii) the value $\lambda=1+5\kappa(\tfrac15)$ is exactly the
least coefficient this argument admits.

For strictness, suppose $R=\Psi$ in this shape; then every estimate above
is an equality. Equality in $\kappa(p_k)\le(\lambda-1)p_k$ with $0<p_k\le\tfrac15$
forces $p_k=\tfrac15$ (the ratio is strictly increasing); this rules
out $a<\tfrac12$ (there $p_k<\tfrac16$), so $a\ge\tfrac12$, and equality in
$\kappa(|2a-1|)\le\kappa(p_k)$ forces $2a-1=\tfrac15$, i.e.\ $a=\tfrac35$ ($\kappa$
strictly increasing on $[0,1]$). The left part then has $\ge3$ symbols, each
$\ge p_k=\tfrac15$, of total mass $\tfrac35$: it is exactly
$(\tfrac15,\tfrac15,\tfrac15)$; also $p_{k+1}=p_k=\tfrac15$. Finally $R=\Phi$
requires equality in the right-part bound \eqref{eq:children}, and the right
part has $\ge3$ symbols, so by the equality clause of the IH its
renormalisation is uniform ternary: $p_{k+1}=\tfrac{1-a}3=\tfrac2{15}$,
contradicting $p_{k+1}=\tfrac15$. Hence $R<\Psi$, and the inequality is strict.
nodes.statement_short: Strong induction on $n$ via the root split, case by case over the shapes. The binding shape $(1,2)$ forces $C$; shape $(3,3)$ forces $\lambda$ via the ratio bound.

nodes.name: Reduction to Phi <= Psi
nodes.statement:
Writing $\Phi$ for the resulting
upper bound on $R$, it suffices in each case to show $\Phi\le\Psi
=p_1+C-\lambda p_n$, tracking where equality can occur.

nodes.name: Dominant leader
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Dominant leader ($p_1\ge\tfrac12$).}
The root splits the leader off on its own; the rest $\rho$ has $n-1\ge2$ symbols and least symbol
$\tfrac{p_n}{1-p_1}$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:univ} gives
$R\le(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1))+(1-p_1)-p_n$. Then, using $p_n\le\tfrac12(1-p_1)$ and
$\lambda>1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R-\Psi\ &\le\ \bigl(2-2p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(\lambda-1)p_n-C\\
  &\le\ h(p_1)-C\ \le\ \tfrac{\lambda-1}{4}-C\ <\ 0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (S2).
nodes.statement_short: For $p_1\ge1/2$ use the universal bound and (S2).

nodes.name: Go through shapes
nodes.statement:
For $p_1<\tfrac12$ we go through the shapes of Lemma~\ref{lem:shapes}. Shapes
$(1,\cdot)$ have $p_1\in[\tfrac13,\tfrac12)$; group shapes have $a<\tfrac23$.
nodes.statement_short: For $p_1<1/2$ go through the shapes of Lemma 6.

nodes.name: Shape (1,2)
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Shape $(1,2)$ (so $n=3$): the binding case.}
Here $\Phi=\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(p_2-p_3)$ and
\[
  \Phi-\Psi=\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+p_2+(\lambda-1)p_3-p_1-C .
\]
Substituting $p_3=1-p_1-p_2$, the middle terms equal
$(2-\lambda)p_2+(\lambda-1)(1-p_1)$, increasing in $p_2$ (since $\lambda<2$); at
the extreme $p_2=p_1$ (so $p_3=1-2p_1$),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Phi-\Psi\ &\le\ \bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+(\lambda-1)(1-2p_1)-C\\
  &=\ \psi(p_1)-C\ \le\ \psi(\tfrac13)-C\ =\ 0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (S1). Equality requires
$p_1=\tfrac13$ and $p_2=p_1$ (the $p_2$-coefficient $2-\lambda$ is
positive) and equality in the chord bound for the right part, i.e.\
$p_2=p_3$: the uniform ternary source. This is the extremal case, and it is
what forces the value of the constant, since $C=\psi(\tfrac13)$ is the
smallest for which the bound can hold.
nodes.statement_short: Binding case: reduces to $\psi(p_1)\le\psi(1/3)=C$; equality only at the uniform ternary source.

nodes.name: Shape (2,3)
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Shape $(2,3)$.}
Here $a=p_1+p_2\in[\tfrac25,\tfrac23)$ and
$\Phi-\Psi=E+(p_1-p_2)+p_3-p_1-a\,C\le E-a\,C$ (since $p_3\le p_2$; the
$\lambda p_n$-terms cancel). On
$[\tfrac25,\tfrac12]$: $E\le(2a-1)^2$ by \eqref{eq:E}, and
$\tfrac{(2a-1)^2}{a}$ has derivative of the sign of $2a-1$, hence is decreasing
there, so $\tfrac Ea\le\tfrac{(1/5)^2}{2/5}<C$. On
$[\tfrac12,\tfrac23)$, (S3) gives
$\tfrac Ea\le6c_3\bigl(1-\tfrac1{2a}\bigr)<\tfrac32c_3<C$. Hence
$E<aC$ and $\Phi<\Psi$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduces to $E<aC$, by the quadratic bound or (S3).

nodes.name: Shape (2,2)
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Shape $(2,2)$ (so $n=4$).}
Here $a=p_1+p_2\in[\tfrac25,\tfrac23)$ and
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Phi-\Psi&=E+(p_1-p_2)+(p_3-p_4)-p_1-C+\lambda p_4\\
   &=E-p_2+p_3+(\lambda-1)p_4-C .
\end{aligned}
\]
With $p_3+p_4=1-a$ fixed,
$-p_2+p_3+(\lambda-1)p_4=-p_2+(2-\lambda)p_3+(\lambda-1)(1-a)$
is increasing in $p_3$ ($\lambda<2$), hence maximal at $p_3=p_2$, where it equals
$(\lambda-1)(1-a-p_2)$; and $p_2\ge p_3\ge\tfrac{1-a}{2}$ gives
$(\lambda-1)(1-a-p_2)\le\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)$. Therefore
$\Phi-\Psi\le E+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)-C$. On $[\tfrac25,\tfrac12]$: with
$E\le(2a-1)^2$, the bound $(2a-1)^2+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)$ is convex with
endpoint values $\tfrac1{25}+\tfrac3{10}(\lambda-1)$ at $a=\tfrac25$ and
$\tfrac{\lambda-1}{4}$ at $a=\tfrac12$, and both are less than $C$:
$\tfrac{\lambda-1}4<C$, while
$\tfrac1{25}+\tfrac3{10}(\lambda-1)-C<0$. On $[\tfrac12,\tfrac23)$:
with (S3), $6c_3(a-\tfrac12)+\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}(1-a)$ has positive slope
$6c_3-\tfrac{\lambda-1}{2}$, so on $a<\tfrac23$,
\[
  \Phi-\Psi\ <\ 6c_3\cdot\tfrac16+\frac{\lambda-1}{2}\cdot\frac13-C
  <\ 0. 
\]
nodes.statement_short: Reduces to a convex bound in $a$ checked at endpoints.

nodes.name: Shape (3,3)
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Shape $(3,3)$.}
Here the $C$-terms and $p_1,p_n$ cancel and
$\Phi-\Psi=E+p_{k+1}-\lambda p_k$. The left part has at least $3$ symbols of
total mass $a$, so its least symbol obeys $p_k\le\tfrac a3$. If $a\ge\tfrac12$,
then \eqref{eq:E} gives $2a-1\le p_k\le\tfrac a3$, whence $a\le\tfrac35$ and
$p_k\le\tfrac15$; if $a<\tfrac12$ then $p_k\le\tfrac a3<\tfrac15$. In
either case $|2a-1|\le p_k\le\tfrac15$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(ii)
($\kappa$ increasing, then the ratio bound),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  E\ &=\ \kappa(2a-1)\ \le\ \kappa(p_k)\ \le\ (\lambda-1)\,p_k ,\\
  \text{so}\quad
  E+p_{k+1}\ &\le\ (\lambda-1)p_k+p_k\ =\ \lambda\,p_k ,
\end{aligned}
\]
using $p_{k+1}\le p_k$: $\Phi\le\Psi$. This case needs no constant at all,
it is what forces the correction coefficient, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(ii) the value $\lambda=1+5\kappa(\tfrac15)$ is exactly the
least coefficient this argument admits.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio bound gives $E+p_{k+1}\le\lambda p_k$; this forces $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Strictness in shape (3,3)
nodes.statement:
For strictness, suppose $R=\Psi$ in this shape; then every estimate above
is an equality. Equality in $\kappa(p_k)\le(\lambda-1)p_k$ with $0<p_k\le\tfrac15$
forces $p_k=\tfrac15$ (the ratio is strictly increasing); this rules
out $a<\tfrac12$ (there $p_k<\tfrac16$), so $a\ge\tfrac12$, and equality in
$\kappa(|2a-1|)\le\kappa(p_k)$ forces $2a-1=\tfrac15$, i.e.\ $a=\tfrac35$ ($\kappa$
strictly increasing on $[0,1]$). The left part then has $\ge3$ symbols, each
$\ge p_k=\tfrac15$, of total mass $\tfrac35$: it is exactly
$(\tfrac15,\tfrac15,\tfrac15)$; also $p_{k+1}=p_k=\tfrac15$. Finally $R=\Phi$
requires equality in the right-part bound \eqref{eq:children}, and the right
part has $\ge3$ symbols, so by the equality clause of the IH its
renormalisation is uniform ternary: $p_{k+1}=\tfrac{1-a}3=\tfrac2{15}$,
contradicting $p_{k+1}=\tfrac15$. Hence $R<\Psi$, and the inequality is strict.
nodes.statement_short: Equality would force incompatible values of $p_{k+1}$ via the IH equality clause.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2: uniform cases
nodes.statement:
These are verified for every minimising cut, so ties are immaterial.

\textbf{Uniform ternary} $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$: either minimising cut
gives $R=1-\mathrm H_2(\tfrac13)=c_3$, while
\[
  \Psi=\tfrac13+C-\tfrac{\lambda}3
      =\tfrac13+\Bigl(c_3+\frac{\lambda-1}{3}\Bigr)-\frac{\lambda}{3}

\]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2: Case A
nodes.statement:
This holds in particular whenever $c\ge\tfrac12$. Write $t:=s-p_2=1-p_1-p_2$
for the mass of the tail $(p_3,\dots,p_n)$ (at least two symbols), and let $R''$
be the redundancy of that tail after renormalisation, $(p_3,\dots,p_n)/t$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:rec} at the root and at $\rho$'s root, together with the
grouping identity $\mathrm H_2(p_1)+s\,\mathrm H_2(p_2/s)=\mathrm H(p_1,p_2,t)$, gives
\begin{equation} R\ =\ \bigl(2-p_1-\mathrm H(p_1,p_2,t)\bigr)+t\,R'' .
\end{equation}
If that tail has $\ge3$ symbols, the
induction hypothesis gives $t\,R''\le p_3+tC-\lambda p_n$; if it has exactly
two symbols, the chord bound gives $t\,R''\le p_3-p_n$, and then
$t\,R''+\lambda p_n\le p_3+(\lambda-1)p_n\le p_3+\tfrac{\lambda-1}2t\le p_3+tC$
(using $p_n\le\tfrac t2$ and $\tfrac{\lambda-1}2<C$). In
either case, $R\le\Psi$ reduces to $G(p_1,p_2)\le0$, where
\[
\begin{aligned}
  G(p_1,p_2)\ :=\ &2-2p_1-\mathrm H(p_1,p_2,t)+p_3-C\,(p_1+p_2),\\
  &\qquad p_3\le\min(p_2,t).
\end{aligned}
\]

\begin{lemma} On the region
$\bigl\{\tfrac13\le p_1\le\tfrac12,\ 1-2p_1\le p_2\le p_1,\
p_3\le\min(p_2,t)\bigr\}$,
\[
  G\ \le\ \beta\ :=\ \tfrac53-\log_23-\tfrac23C\ <\ 0 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$G$ is increasing in $p_3$, so put $p_3=\min(p_2,t)$; the junction is
$p_2=\tfrac{1-p_1}2$ (where $p_2=t$), which lies in $[1-2p_1,\,p_1]$ exactly for
$p_1\ge\tfrac13$. On each of the two $p_2$-segments, $G$ is
``affine $-$ entropy of affine arguments'', hence convex in $p_2$; so its
maximum is at $p_2\in\{1-2p_1,\ \tfrac{1-p_1}2,\ p_1\}$. This leaves three
one-variable functions of $p_1$, each again convex (same reason), so each is
maximised at $p_1\in\{\tfrac13,\tfrac12\}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $p_2=1-2p_1$ (then $t=p_1$, $p_3=1-2p_1$):
  at $p_1=\tfrac13$ the value is
  $2-\tfrac23-\log_23+\tfrac13-\tfrac23C=\tfrac53-\log_23-\tfrac23C=\beta$;
  at $p_1=\tfrac12$ it is $1-\mathrm H(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)+0-\tfrac{C}2
  =-\tfrac{C}2<0$.
\item $p_2=\tfrac{1-p_1}2$ (then $p_3=t=p_2$):
  at $p_1=\tfrac13$ the value is again $\beta$ (all three symbols
  $\tfrac13$); at $p_1=\tfrac12$ it is
  $1-\mathrm H(\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)+\tfrac14-\tfrac34C
  =-\tfrac14-\tfrac34C<0$.
\item $p_2=p_1$ (then $p_3=1-2p_1$): this function is pointwise $\le$ the first
  one, since it has the same entropy term (by symmetry of $\mathrm H$) and the
  same $p_3$, but the larger subtraction $C\cdot2p_1\ge C\,(1-p_1)$ for
  $p_1\ge\tfrac13$.
\end{itemize}
The two $\tfrac12$-endpoint values are $\le\beta$: indeed
$-\tfrac14-\tfrac34C<-\tfrac{C}2$, and
\[
  \beta+\frac{C}2\ =\ \frac53-\log_23-\frac{C}6\ >\ 0 .
\]
Hence $G\le\beta$ on the whole region, and $\beta<0$ by simple arithmetic.
\end{proof}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2: Case B1
nodes.statement:
Here the induction hypothesis on $\rho$ ($\ge3$ symbols) suffices:
$s\,R(\rho)\le p_2+sC-\lambda p_n$, so, using $p_2\le\tfrac s3$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  R-\Psi\ &\le\ \bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+p_2-p_1-C p_1\\
  &\le\ \bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)\bigr)+\tfrac{1-p_1}3-(1+C)\,p_1\ =:\ b(p_1).
\end{aligned}
\]
$b'(p_1)=\log_2\tfrac{p_1}{1-p_1}-\tfrac43-C<0$ on $[\tfrac13,\tfrac12)$ (the
logarithm is negative), so
\[
  b\ \le\ b(\tfrac13)\ =\ c_3-\tfrac19-\tfrac{C}3
  \ <\ 0.
\]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2: Case B2 and conclusion
nodes.statement:
In absolute masses, let $\rho$ split into $L'=(p_2,\dots,p_m)$, $m\ge3$, of
mass $A$, and $R''=(p_{m+1},\dots,p_n)$ with mass $s-A$. Three preliminary
observations.

\textbf{(i) $L'$ is a dominant block.} Lemma~\ref{lem:key} applied to the block
$(p_2,\dots,p_n)$ gives $|2A-s|\le p_m$; since $c>\tfrac13$ means $s<3p_2$,
\[
  A\ \le\ \tfrac{s+p_m}2\ \le\ \tfrac{s+p_2}2\ <\ 2p_2,
\]
so $p_2/A>\tfrac12$, and within $L'$ its most probable symbol is again split off on its own. By the block
form of Corollary~\ref{cor:isob} and the grouping rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &A\,R_{L'}\ \le\ 2A-p_2-A\,\mathrm H_2\bigl(\tfrac{p_2}A\bigr),\\
  &\mathrm H(p_1,A,s{-}A)+A\,\mathrm H_2\bigl(\tfrac{p_2}A\bigr)
  =\mathrm H(p_1,p_2,A{-}p_2,s{-}A)
\end{aligned}
\]
(when $|L'|=2$ the displayed bound is immediate from $R_{L'}=1-\mathrm H_2(p_2/A)$ and
$p_2\le A$).

\textbf{(ii) $R''$ is not a singleton.} If it were $\{p_n\}$, the cut after symbol
$n-1$ would have been chosen; but the cut after symbol $2$ (available since
$n-1\ge3$) has imbalance $s-2p_2\le s-2p_n$, with equality only if
$p_2=p_n$, which would make all of $p_2,\dots,p_n$ equal, forcing
$c=p_2/s=\tfrac1{n-1}\le\tfrac13$ and contradicting $c>\tfrac13$. So the cut
after symbol $2$ is strictly better, a contradiction (no tie rule is invoked). If $|R''|=2$,
the chord bound, $p_n\le\tfrac{s-A}2$ and $\tfrac{\lambda-1}2<C$ give, as in
Case A, $(s-A)R''+\lambda p_n\le p_{m+1}+(s-A)C$; if $|R''|\ge3$ the induction
hypothesis gives the same.

\textbf{(iii)} Combining (i) and (ii) with the two-level expansion \eqref{eq:2level}
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rec} applied at the root and at $\rho$'s root), the requirement
$R\le\Psi$ reduces to $\Delta\le0$, where
\begin{equation} \begin{split}
  \Delta\ :=\ &2-2p_1+2A-p_2-\mathrm H\bigl(p_1,p_2,A{-}p_2,s{-}A\bigr)\\
  &+p_{m+1}-C\,(p_1+A).
\end{split}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[The B2 inequality] $\Delta\le\max\bigl(\beta,-\tfrac1{45}\bigr)<0$ for
every tuple $(p_1,p_2,A,q,r)$
\textup{(}$q=p_m$, $r=p_{m+1}$\textup{)} satisfying
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &\textup{(P1) }\tfrac13\le p_1\le\tfrac12;\quad
  \textup{(P2) }2p_1+p_2\ge1;\\
  &\textup{(P3) }\tfrac s3\le p_2\le\tfrac s2;\quad
  \textup{(P4) }0\le q\le A-p_2;
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
  \textup{(P5) }|2A-s|\le q;\qquad
  \textup{(P6) }0\le r\le q\qquad (s=1-p_1).
\]
Every case-\textup{B2} configuration satisfies \textup{(P1)--(P6)}: \textup{(P1),
(P2)} by Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}, \textup{(P3)} from $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$,
\textup{(P4)} because the left block $(p_2,\dots,p_m)$ has mass $A$, so $A-p_2=p_3+\cdots+p_m$ is a sum of symbols one of which is $q=p_m$ and the rest nonnegative, giving $0<q\le A-p_2$; \textup{(P5)} by
Lemma~\ref{lem:key}, \textup{(P6)} by sorting.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\textbf{Step 1 (change of variables).} Set $x=p_1$, $y=p_2$, $u=A-p_2$,
$v=s-A$; then $x+y+u+v=1$ and $x,y,u\ge0$. From (P4), (P5):
$2A-s\le q\le u$ gives $y+u-v\le u$, i.e.\ $v\ge y$; and $s-2A\le q\le u$ gives
$v\le y+2u$. In these variables, using $r\le q\le u$ (P6), (P4) and that
$\Delta$ is nondecreasing in $r$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Delta\ \le\ F(x,y,u)\ &:=\ 2-2x+y+3u-\mathrm H(x,y,u,v)\\
  &\phantom{{}:={}}-C\,(x+y+u),\\
  &\phantom{{}:={}}v=1-x-y-u .
\end{aligned}
\]

\textbf{Step 2 (the polytope).} Conditions (P1)--(P3), together with the two consequences $v\ge y$ and $v\le y+2u$ of (P5) from Step 1,
translate to: $\tfrac13\le x\le\tfrac12$; $2x+y\ge1$; $x+3y\ge1$; $x+2y\le1$;
$x+2y+u\le1$ ($v\ge y$); $x+2y+3u\ge1$ ($v\le y+2u$). Call this polytope
$\mathcal{P}$ (note $u\ge0$ is implied by the last two with $x+2y\le1$).

\textbf{Step 3 (convexity).} $F$ is affine minus
$\mathrm H(x,y,u,v)=\sum_k\mathrm I(a_k)$, a sum of the concave function

nodes.name: (i) L' is a dominant block
nodes.statement:
\textbf{(i) $L'$ is a dominant block.} Lemma~\ref{lem:key} applied to the block
$(p_2,\dots,p_n)$ gives $|2A-s|\le p_m$; since $c>\tfrac13$ means $s<3p_2$,
\[
  A\ \le\ \tfrac{s+p_m}2\ \le\ \tfrac{s+p_2}2\ <\ 2p_2,
\]

form of Corollary~\ref{cor:isob} and the grouping rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  &A\,R_{L'}\ \le\ 2A-p_2-A\,\mathrm H_2\bigl(\tfrac{p_2}A\bigr),\\
  &\mathrm H(p_1,A,s{-}A)+A\,\mathrm H_2\bigl(\tfrac{p_2}A\bigr)

\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.statement_short: Key lemma gives $p_2/A>1/2$, so the isolation ceiling bounds $AR_{L'}$.

\textbf{(ii) $R''$ is not a singleton.} If it were $\{p_n\}$, the cut after symbol
$n-1$ would have been chosen; but the cut after symbol $2$ (available since
$n-1\ge3$) has imbalance $s-2p_2\le s-2p_n$, with equality only if
$p_2=p_n$, which would make all of $p_2,\dots,p_n$ equal, forcing
$c=p_2/s=\tfrac1{n-1}\le\tfrac13$ and contradicting $c>\tfrac13$. So the cut
after symbol $2$ is strictly better, a contradiction (no tie rule is invoked). If $|R''|=2$,

hypothesis gives the same.

$M=x+y+u$, so that $C M=4M-\tfrac53M\log_25$; with
$\log_26=1+\log_23$, $\log_2{15}=\log_23+\log_25$, $\log_2{18}=1+2\log_23$,
$\log_2\tfrac52=\log_25-1$, $\log_2\tfrac{18}5=1+2\log_23-\log_25$, direct evaluation
gives
\[
\begin{array}{l}
F(W_1)=-1-\log_23+\tfrac{10}9\log_25=\beta,\\[3pt]
F(W_2)=-\tfrac23-\tfrac25\log_23+\tfrac49\log_25,\\[3pt]
F(W_3)=-\tfrac45+\tfrac13\log_25,\\[3pt]
F(W_4)=-\tfrac{23}9-\tfrac56\log_23+\tfrac{40}{27}\log_25,\\[3pt]
F(W_5)=-\tfrac83-\tfrac12\log_23+\tfrac{25}{18}\log_25,\\[3pt]
F(W_6)=-\tfrac{13}4+\tfrac54\log_25 .
\end{array}
\]

substituting $\log_23>\tfrac{19}{12}$, $\log_25<\tfrac73$ gives
\begin{align*}
  F(W_2)&\le\tfrac{-180-171+280}{270}=-\tfrac{71}{270},\\
  F(W_3)&\le-\tfrac45+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac73=-\tfrac1{45},\\
  F(W_4)&\le\tfrac{-1656-855+2240}{648}=-\tfrac{271}{648},\\
  F(W_5)&\le\tfrac{-576-171+700}{216}=-\tfrac{47}{216},\\
  F(W_6)&\le-\tfrac{13}4+\tfrac{35}{12}=-\tfrac13,
\end{align*}
so $F(W_j)\le-\tfrac1{45}$ for $j=2,\dots,6$; and $F(W_1)=\beta<0$, critical at the same
balanced configuration $p_1=p_2=\tfrac13$ as in Case~A. Hence
$\Delta\le F\le\max\bigl(\beta,-\tfrac1{45}\bigr)<0$ on $\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: Change variables, bound by a convex $F$ on a polytope covered by six points, evaluate at those points. The key step shows the polytope lies in the hull of $W_1,\dots,W_6$.

nodes.name: Step 1: change of variables
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1 (change of variables).} Set $x=p_1$, $y=p_2$, $u=A-p_2$,
$v=s-A$; then $x+y+u+v=1$ and $x,y,u\ge0$. From (P4), (P5):
$2A-s\le q\le u$ gives $y+u-v\le u$, i.e.\ $v\ge y$; and $s-2A\le q\le u$ gives
$v\le y+2u$. In these variables, using $r\le q\le u$ (P6), (P4) and that
$\Delta$ is nondecreasing in $r$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Delta\ \le\ F(x,y,u)\ &:=\ 2-2x+y+3u-\mathrm H(x,y,u,v)\\
  &\phantom{{}:={}}-C\,(x+y+u),\\
  &\phantom{{}:={}}v=1-x-y-u .
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: Change to $(x,y,u,v)$ and bound $\Delta$ by $F(x,y,u)$.

nodes.name: Step 2: the polytope
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 2 (the polytope).} Conditions (P1)--(P3), together with the two consequences $v\ge y$ and $v\le y+2u$ of (P5) from Step 1,
translate to: $\tfrac13\le x\le\tfrac12$; $2x+y\ge1$; $x+3y\ge1$; $x+2y\le1$;
$x+2y+u\le1$ ($v\ge y$); $x+2y+3u\ge1$ ($v\le y+2u$). Call this polytope
$\mathcal{P}$ (note $u\ge0$ is implied by the last two with $x+2y\le1$).
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: Constraints define the polytope $\mathcal P$.

nodes.name: Step 3: convexity
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 3 (convexity).} $F$ is affine minus
$\mathrm H(x,y,u,v)=\sum_k\mathrm I(a_k)$, a sum of the concave function
$\mathrm I$ evaluated at the affine arguments $a_k\in\{x,y,u,v\}$; hence
$-\mathrm H$, and with it $F$, is convex on $\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is affine minus entropy, hence convex.

nodes.name: Step 4: hull of six points
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 4 (a hull of six points).} We show that $\mathcal{P}$ lies in the convex hull of the six points $W_1,\dots,W_6$, where
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  W_1&=\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,0\bigr),&
  W_2&=\bigl(\tfrac25,\tfrac15,\tfrac1{15}\bigr),&
  W_3&=\bigl(\tfrac25,\tfrac15,\tfrac15\bigr),\\
  W_4&=\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac16,\tfrac1{18}\bigr),&
  W_5&=\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac16,\tfrac16\bigr),&
  W_6&=\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac14,0\bigr).
  \end{aligned}
\]
The idea is to project $\mathcal{P}$ onto the $(x,y)$-plane and then lift back.
Eliminating $u$, the pair $(x,y)$ ranges over the planar region
$\{\tfrac13\le x\le\tfrac12,\ y^-(x)\le y\le y^+(x)\}$ with
$y^+(x)=\tfrac{1-x}2$ and $y^-(x)=\max\bigl(1-2x,\tfrac{1-x}3\bigr)$, the two
bounds crossing at $x=\tfrac25$. This region is the quadrilateral with corners
$Q_1=(\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$, $Q_2=(\tfrac25,\tfrac15)$, $Q_3=(\tfrac12,\tfrac16)$,
$Q_4=(\tfrac12,\tfrac14)$: its upper edge $y=y^+(x)$ is the segment $Q_1Q_4$,
and its lower edge $y=y^-(x)$ is the segment $Q_1Q_2$ for $x\le\tfrac25$ and
$Q_2Q_3$ for $x\ge\tfrac25$, as the parametrisations
\[
  \bigl(x,y^+(x)\bigr)=(1-\lambda)Q_1+\lambda Q_4,\qquad \lambda=6x-2,
\]
\[
  \bigl(x,y^-(x)\bigr)=
  \begin{cases}
  (1-\lambda)Q_1+\lambda Q_2,\quad \lambda=15x-5, & x\le\tfrac25,\\
  (1-\lambda)Q_2+\lambda Q_3,\quad \lambda=10x-4, & x\ge\tfrac25,
  \end{cases}
\]
show; hence every $(x,y)$ in the region is a convex combination of
$Q_1,\dots,Q_4$. To lift back to $\mathcal{P}$, fix such an $(x,y)$: the constraints
$x+2y+u\le1$ and $x+2y+3u\ge1$ confine $u$ to the interval
$\bigl[\tfrac{1-x-2y}3,\ 1-x-2y\bigr]$, whose two endpoints are affine in
$(x,y)$. Writing $u$ as a convex combination of these two endpoints, and
substituting for $(x,y)$ its expression as a convex combination of the $Q_i$,
exhibits $(x,y,u)$ as a convex combination of the six points
$\bigl(Q_i,\tfrac{1-x-2y}3\big|_{Q_i}\bigr)$ and
$\bigl(Q_i,(1-x-2y)\big|_{Q_i}\bigr)$. Since $1-x-2y$ equals
$0,\tfrac15,\tfrac16,0$ at $Q_1,\dots,Q_4$, these six points are exactly
$W_1,\dots,W_6$.
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mathcal P$ lies in the convex hull of $W_1,\dots,W_6$.

nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate $F$ at the six points; all $\le\max(\beta,-1/45)$.

nodes.name: Both B2 constraint families are essential
nodes.statement:
Both constraint families in Lemma~\ref{lem:B2} are essential: dropping
isolation (P2) admits
$(p_1,p_2,A,q,r)=(\tfrac13,\tfrac29,\tfrac49,\tfrac29,\tfrac29)$ with
$\Delta=\tfrac{26}9-\tfrac53\log_23-\tfrac79C>0$, and dropping
the split constraint
(P5) admits $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac23,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ with
$\Delta=\tfrac83-\log_23-C>0$.
The Shannon--Fano optimality of the cut is thus the
mechanism that makes \eqref{eq:B2} true, entering the proof only through its
two linear consequences $y\le v\le y+2u$.
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: Dropping isolation (P2) or the split constraint (P5) gives $\Delta>0$: Fano cut optimality is what makes (8) true.

nodes.name: Induction closes
nodes.statement:
Cases A, B1, B2 exhaust shape $(1,3)$ (if $\rho$ does not isolate its leader
then $c<\tfrac12$), each with strict inequality, so, together with
\S\ref{ss:induct}--\ref{ss:unif}, the induction closes; every case is strict:
the dominant case, shapes $(2,3)$, $(2,2)$, $(3,3)$ (the latter via the
equality clause of the IH), the three cases of shape $(1,3)$, and the uniform
quinary source, except shape $(1,2)$, which is tight exactly at the
uniform ternary source, where equality indeed holds (\S\ref{ss:unif}).
Theorem~\ref{thm:aff}, and with it the affine branch of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, are proved; the middle branches are the topic of
the next section. \qed
nodes.section: Case B2: $\rho$ splits as a group, $\tfrac13<c<\tfrac12$
nodes.statement_short: All cases are strict except shape $(1,2)$ at the uniform ternary source; Theorem 2 follows.

nodes.name: delta and the block bound V
nodes.statement:
Throughout this section
\[
\begin{aligned}
  K\ &:=\ \tfrac52-\tfrac56\log_25\ =\ \tfrac{1+C}{2}\ =\ 0.565059\ldots,\\
  \delta\ &:=\ 1-2p_1,\qquad V(q)\ :=\ 2-q-\mathrm H_2(q),
\end{aligned}
\]
$V$ is the tight bound of
Corollary~\ref{cor:isob} for a block whose leader fraction is $q\ge\tfrac12$
(convex, since $-\mathrm H_2$ is convex).
nodes.statement_short: Set $\delta=1-2p_1$; $K=(1+C)/2$ and $V(q)=2-q-\mathrm H_2(q)$, the isolation ceiling of a block.

nodes.name: Auxiliary curve B-tilde
nodes.statement:
The auxiliary single curve
\[
  \tilde B(p_1)\ :=\ 1+(1+C)\,p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)
  \qquad\bigl(\tfrac13\le p_1\le\tfrac12\bigr)
\]
will lie above all the comparison curves at once; the two branches of the
envelope itself are introduced after Lemma~\ref{lem:midcomp}.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde B(p_1)=1+(1+C)p_1-\mathrm H_2(p_1)$ on $[1/3,1/2]$, to dominate all comparison curves.

nodes.name: Values and monotonicity of B-tilde
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde B(1/3)=2-\log_2 3+C/3$, $\tilde B(1/2)=K$, and $\tilde B$ is strictly increasing.

nodes.name: Fine group bounds
nodes.statement:
Let $\tfrac13\le p_1<\tfrac12$ and let the root split be a group split
($2p_1+p_2<1$) with left mass $a$; put $x:=a-p_1>0$ and, for $0<x<1-p_1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  F(p_1,x)\ &:=\ 1+p_1+2x+(1-p_1-x)\,C\\
  &\phantom{{}:={}}-\mathrm H\bigl(p_1,x,1-p_1-x\bigr),\\
  G(p_1,x)\ &:=\ F(p_1,x)+x\,C .
\end{aligned}
\]
If the left part has exactly two symbols, then $R<F(p_1,x)$ and
$x\in[\tfrac\delta3,\delta]$; if it has at least three, then $R<G(p_1,x)$ and
$x\in[\tfrac{2\delta}5,\tfrac{2\delta}3]$. Consequently
\[
  R\ <\ \max\Bigl\{F\bigl(p_1,\tfrac\delta3\bigr),\ F(p_1,\delta),\
  G\bigl(p_1,\tfrac{2\delta}5\bigr),\ G\bigl(p_1,\tfrac{2\delta}3\bigr)\Bigr\}.
\]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement:
The left part has at least two symbols: its leader is $p_1$, and its remainder
$L'$ has mass $x$, largest symbol $p_2$ and least symbol $p_k$ ($k$ is the cut
position), so $p_k\le x$. Lemma~\ref{lem:key} at the root reads
$|2a-1|=|2x-\delta|\le p_k$. Since $|2x-\delta|\le x$ gives $x\le\delta$,
i.e.\ $a\le1-p_1\le2p_1$ (as $p_1\ge\tfrac13$), the leader's fraction of the
left part is $p_1/a\ge\tfrac12$, so the leader is again split off on its own within the left part
(Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}); this reduction applied inside the left part and the
grouping identity
$(1-\mathrm H_2(a))+a\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1/a)\bigr)=(1+a)-\mathrm H(p_1,x,1-a)$ give
\[
  R=(1+a)-\mathrm H(p_1,x,1-a)+x\,R_{L'}+(1-a)\,R_{\mathrm{Rt}},
\]
where $R_{L'}$ and $R_{\mathrm{Rt}}$ are the redundancies of the renormalised left remainder $L'$ (mass $x$) and right part $\mathrm{Rt}$ (mass $1-a$, largest symbol $p_{k+1}$). By
Corollary~\ref{cor:aff} (every source),
$(1-a)R_{\mathrm{Rt}}<p_{k+1}+(1-a)C$ (or $=0$ for a singleton, when the
same bound holds trivially).

\textbf{Two left symbols.} Then $L'=\{p_2\}$, so $x=p_2=p_k$ and $xR_{L'}=0$;
with $p_{k+1}\le p_k=x$,
\[
  R\ <\ (1+a)-\mathrm H(p_1,x,1-a)+x+(1-a)\,C\ =\ F(p_1,x),
\]
and $|2x-\delta|\le p_k=x$ reads $x\ge\tfrac\delta3$
\textup{(}$\delta-2x\le x$\textup{)} and $x\le\delta$
\textup{(}$2x-\delta\le x$\textup{)}.

\textbf{At least three left symbols.} Then $|L'|\ge2$ and $xR_{L'}<p_2+xC$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:aff} again); since $p_2$ and $p_k$ are distinct symbols of
$L'$, $p_2+p_{k+1}\le p_2+p_k\le x$, whence $R<F(p_1,x)+xC=G(p_1,x)$.
Moreover $p_k\le\min(p_2,\,x-p_2)\le\tfrac x2$, so $|2x-\delta|\le\tfrac x2$:
$x\ge\tfrac{2\delta}5$ and $x\le\tfrac{2\delta}3$.

For the endpoints, in $x$, with $t:=1-p_1-x$ and $\mathrm I'(t)=-\log_2 t-\log_2 e$,
\[
  \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\ =\ 2-C+\log_2\frac{x}{t},
  \qquad
  \frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\ =\ 2+\log_2\frac{x}{t},
\]
both strictly increasing in $x$ ($x$ increases, $t$ decreases); so
$F(p_1,\cdot)$ and $G(p_1,\cdot)$ are decreasing-then-increasing and each is
maximised over its $x$-interval at an endpoint.
nodes.statement_short: The leader is isolated inside the left part; bound the children by the affine bound and use the key lemma to confine $x$; endpoints by monotone derivatives.

nodes.name: Two-level identity
nodes.statement:

$L'$ has mass $x$, largest symbol $p_2$ and least symbol $p_k$ ($k$ is the cut
position), so $p_k\le x$. Lemma~\ref{lem:key} at the root reads
$|2a-1|=|2x-\delta|\le p_k$. Since $|2x-\delta|\le x$ gives $x\le\delta$,
i.e.\ $a\le1-p_1\le2p_1$ (as $p_1\ge\tfrac13$), the leader's fraction of the
left part is $p_1/a\ge\tfrac12$, so the leader is again split off on its own within the left part
(Lemma~\ref{lem:iso}); this reduction applied inside the left part and the
grouping identity
$(1-\mathrm H_2(a))+a\bigl(1-\mathrm H_2(p_1/a)\bigr)=(1+a)-\mathrm H(p_1,x,1-a)$ give
\[

\]
